title: Caring for the environment: soil, forests and one shared home
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 5 'Our School — A Happy Place' (a green school: waste, water, trees; kindness, respect and positive behaviour), NCERT Class 5 'Earth — Our Shared Home' (Earth as a connected living planet; sharing nature, knowledge and culture; Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam) and NIOS Class 5 'Conservation of Soil and Forests' (soil erosion, its harm and prevention; soil pollution; why forests must be protected). No textbook needed.
summary: A few centimetres of topsoil can take hundreds of years to form, and one monsoon can wash it away. Your child starts with the Earth seen from space, then looks closely at soil: its layers, how wind and water carry it off, and how farmers hold it with terraces, check dams and trees. They count the life in a handful of soil, weigh up organic and chemical farming, measure how shade and white surfaces keep a place cool, and audit their own home as a 'green explorer'. They trap heat in a jar as Eunice Foote did in 1856. Amur falcons from Mongolia, chillies from Mexico and the zero from India show that living things, foods and ideas cross every border. The lesson ends with the old Indian idea that the whole Earth is one family.
builds_on: Class 2: habitats, litter, the three Rs, nature reserves. Class 3: food chains and webs, decomposers, keystone species, pollution, roots holding soil, saving water. This rung goes into soil erosion and soil pollution properly, forests, heat islands, the greenhouse effect, a green audit, and the Earth as one connected home. Later: climate change, ecosystems and the carbon cycle in middle school.
goals: By the end your child can explain what topsoil is, why it takes so long to form, and how water and wind erode it.
By the end your child can show at least four ways farmers prevent erosion, using a model.
By the end your child can name causes of soil pollution and explain how compost and living soil keep it healthy, and give both sides of the organic farming debate.
By the end your child can give several reasons forests must be protected, and say whose lives depend on them.
By the end your child can carry out a green audit of their home or school and make one real change.
By the end your child can explain the greenhouse effect with the jar experiment, and give examples of how birds, seeds, air and ideas cross borders.
subconcepts: topsoil forms very slowly and feeds almost all land life
soil erosion by water and wind
harm from erosion: poor farms, muddy rivers, landslides
preventing erosion: terraces, bunds, check dams, cover crops, trees
soil pollution: plastic, pesticides, too much fertiliser, factory waste
healthy soil is alive: compost and soil creatures
why forests matter: water, soil, climate, homes and people
shade and white roofs cool places (heat islands)
a green audit: waste, water, energy, trees and kindness
nature has no borders: migrating birds, travelling seeds and air
foods, ideas and knowledge travel and are shared
Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam: the Earth as one family
dignity of labour: respecting the people who care for our places
words: topsoil
the dark, crumbly top layer of soil, full of life and nutrients, where plants grow
soil erosion
topsoil being carried away by water or wind
terrace
a flat step cut into a hillside for farming, so rain can't wash the soil down
check dam
a small wall across a stream that slows water and catches soil
soil pollution
harmful things in soil, like plastic, poisons or too much chemical fertiliser
compost
rotted plant and food waste that makes soil rich
heat island
a city area that is much hotter than the land around it because of roads, roofs and few trees

days.title: Our address in the universe
days.goal: Recall Class 3, see the Earth from space, read the story, and find the layers in soil.

steps.title: What do we remember?
steps.do: Recall the Class 3 lesson in one quick round. Ask: 'What do decomposers do?' (They eat dead plants and animals and turn them back into soil.) 'What happened when India's vultures disappeared?' (Dead animals lay rotting, stray dogs increased, and so did rabies.) 'What did the tray of bare soil show?' (Without roots and leaves, rain washes soil away.) Say: 'This time we start in space and end in a handful of soil.'

steps.title: The Earth from space
steps.do: Show a photo of the Earth from space, in an atlas or on a phone. The 1972 'Blue Marble' photo is a good one. Say: 'In 1984 Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian in space. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi asked him how India looked from up there. He answered: Saare jahan se achha, better than the whole world.' Ask: 'Can you see any borders between countries in the photo? What can you see?' (Oceans, clouds, deserts, forests and ice, but no lines.) Then your child writes their full address, adding after the country: Asia, Earth, the Solar System, the Milky Way.

steps.title: Story: The Sky Over Doyang
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Whose bird was the falcon?' and 'What changed Achumi's mind?' Keep the answers for Day 7.

steps.title: Soil layers in a jar
steps.do: Put two handfuls of soil, from a plant pot or any patch of ground, into a clear glass jar. Fill the jar with water nearly to the top. Close the lid tightly, and your child shakes it hard for one minute. Ask: 'What will happen when we leave it still? Why?' Leave the jar still until tomorrow. Small stones and sand sink first, then finer silt, then a thin layer of clay. Bits of dead leaf float on top. Say: 'In the ground, the top layer is called topsoil. It is dark because it is full of humus: rotted leaves and dead creatures. Below it is lighter, harder subsoil, and below that, rock.' If you have a garden, dig a hole about 30 cm deep and look at its side to see these layers.

steps.title: How long does soil take?
steps.do: Say: 'Soil is made when rock is slowly broken by heat, cold, water and roots, and mixed with rotted plants and animals. It often takes hundreds of years to make just a few centimetres of topsoil, about the length of your little finger.' Ask: 'One heavy monsoon washes 2 cm of soil off a bare field. How long will nature take to make it again?' (Hundreds of years. Soil can be lost far faster than it forms.)

need: a photo of the Earth from space (atlas or phone)
a clear glass jar with a lid
two handfuls of soil and water

days.title: Wind and water carry soil away
days.goal: Watch wind erode soil, build a hill farm that holds its soil, and meet the scientist who warned about dust storms.

steps.title: Wind on dry, damp and covered soil
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Put three small heaps of soil on three steel plates: dry soil, damp soil, and dry soil covered with dry leaves. Spread newspaper around each plate. Ask: 'Which heap will lose the most soil? Why?' Your child blows hard through a straw at each heap for 10 seconds, from the same distance. Compare how far the soil spreads. Ask: 'Where in India might wind carry soil away?' (Dry, bare places, such as parts of Rajasthan, in the hot, windy months before the monsoon.)

steps.title: A hill farm that holds its soil
steps.do: Do Activity a1, in the bathroom or on the balcony. Build two equal hills of damp soil on two trays, and tilt each tray on a book with a cup at the low end. Leave one hill smooth and bare. On the other, press steps into the side with a ruler (terraces), put rows of pebbles across the slope (bunds), a small stone wall across a channel (a check dam), and stick in twigs and grass as trees and cover. Ask: 'Which hill will lose more mud?' Pour the same 'rain' on both from a bottle with holes in the cap. Compare the mud in the cups. Ask: 'What did each thing do?' (Terraces stop the water on flat steps so it soaks in. Bunds and check dams slow the water and catch soil. Roots hold the soil.) Say: 'Farmers in the Himalayas, the Western Ghats and the Nilgiris have farmed on terraces for centuries.'

steps.title: The scientist who warned about the dust
steps.do: Talk about voice v1, Hugh Hammond Bennett and the Dust Bowl. Ask first: 'What do you think happens when grassland is ploughed up and then a long drought comes?' Then tell the story and ask the voice question.

need: three steel plates, soil, dry leaves, newspaper, a straw
two trays, damp soil, a ruler, pebbles, twigs and grass, two books, two cups
a plastic bottle with holes in the cap

days.title: Poisoned soil and living soil
days.goal: Count the life in soil, find out what pollutes it, and weigh up organic and chemical farming.

steps.title: How much life is in a handful of soil?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Take one handful of soil from a plant pot or from under a tree, where dead leaves have lain for a while. Take a second handful of dry dust from a swept corner or the roadside. Ask: 'Which handful will have more living things? Why?' Spread each on white paper and look for 5 minutes, with a magnifying glass or the zoom on a phone camera. Count every living thing: ants, worms, springtails (tiny jumping specks), mites, white fungus threads. Then ask: 'Which soil is more alive? Why?' Say: 'A pinch of healthy soil also holds millions of bacteria, far too small to see.'

steps.title: What poisons soil?
steps.do: Make two lists together. What harms soil: plastic bags and wrappers that don't rot and keep water and air out; pesticides that kill soil creatures as well as pests; too much chemical fertiliser, which can harm soil life and wash into rivers and wells; oil, paint and battery waste; and factory waste dumped on land. What helps soil: compost, cow-dung manure, green manure (plants grown and dug back in), changing crops each season, and leaving fallen leaves. Ask: 'Why do earthworms matter to a farmer?' (They mix the soil, make tunnels for air and water, and turn dead leaves into rich soil.)

steps.title: Organic or chemical? A real debate
steps.do: Talk about voice v2. Your child argues for organic farming for 2 minutes, then for chemical fertilisers for 2 minutes. Then tell the two true stories. Sikkim changed to organic farming slowly, over more than ten years, and became India's first fully organic state in 2016. Sri Lanka banned chemical fertilisers almost overnight in 2021. Harvests of rice and tea fell sharply, and the ban was reversed within months. Ask the voice question. Then ask: 'Experts still disagree. What would you want to measure to find out?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1: soil, erosion and soil pollution. Read each question aloud if needed.

need: two handfuls of soil from different places
white paper and a magnifying glass (or a phone camera)

days.title: Forests and the cool shade
days.goal: Measure how trees and white roofs cool a place, and find out whose lives depend on forests.

steps.title: Black paper, white paper, shade
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. In the late morning, put a black and a white sheet of paper side by side in full sun, on a balcony or a sunny windowsill. Put a second black sheet in the shade nearby. Ask: 'Which will be hottest? Will the black paper in the shade get hot?' After 15 minutes, your child feels each with the back of the hand. Ask: 'Which is hottest? Which is coolest? Why?' Then explain. Dark surfaces absorb more sunlight and get hot. White ones reflect most of it. Trees give shade, and they also cool the air, because water evaporates from their leaves. So a city with many dark roads and roofs and few trees becomes a heat island, often several degrees hotter than the land around it. Say: 'In Ahmedabad and Hyderabad, many roofs are now being painted white to keep homes cooler in heat waves.'

steps.title: Why forests matter
steps.do: Ask: 'Why do forests matter?' Make a big list together. Roots hold the soil. Forests soak up rain and feed springs and rivers. They cool the air and help make rain. They store carbon in their wood. They give fruit, honey, medicines and wood. Most kinds of land animals and plants live in forests. Then the challenge: 'People call the Amazon rainforest the lungs of the Earth, making 20% of our oxygen. Is that true?' Discuss the challenge hint.

steps.title: Tree pose
steps.do: Stand in vrikshasana, the tree pose: one foot pressed against the inside of the other leg, palms together above the head. Hold it for five slow breaths. Ask: 'Where did the oxygen in your breath come from?' (From plants on land and from tiny living things in the sea, which make oxygen from sunlight.) Say: 'And the carbon dioxide you breathe out is used by plants to make their food.'

steps.title: Forest people
steps.do: Say: 'Millions of people in India, many of them Adivasi communities, live in or beside forests and have cared for them for generations. The Soligas live in the forests of the BR Hills in Karnataka. The Bishnois of Rajasthan protect khejri trees and blackbuck. The Khasi people of Meghalaya keep sacred groves. In 2006 India passed the Forest Rights Act. It says forest communities have rights to the land and forest they have always used.' Ask: 'Who should decide what happens to a forest: the government, a company, the people who live in it, or the animals?' Listen, then say: 'Bishnoi tradition tells that in 1730, at Khejarli, Amrita Devi and hundreds of Bishnois gave their lives trying to stop the king's men cutting their trees.' Ask: 'Is a tree worth that much?'

days.title: Green explorers: auditing our place
days.goal: Audit your home or school for waste, water, energy, greenery and kindness, and choose one real change.

steps.title: The green audit
steps.do: Do Activity a2, the project's first step. Your child is the Green Explorer of your home, building or school. With a clipboard, they check and score five things: waste (are wet and dry bins separate? how full?), water (any drips? is rainwater caught?), energy (lights and fans left on in empty rooms? old bulbs that use more electricity than LED bulbs?), greenery (how many trees and plants? any bare soil?), and people (who cleans? who repairs? does everyone have a safe, shady place?). They give each a score from 1 to 5 and write one problem for each.

steps.title: Who keeps this place clean?
steps.do: Ask: 'In your audit, who does the cleaning, the sweeping, the repairs and the waste collection? Do we know their names?' If you can, go and talk with one of them: the sweeper, the guard, the gardener or the waste collector. Ask what makes their work harder (mixed waste, litter, rudeness) and what makes it easier. Afterwards, ask: 'Is a place green if it is clean for some people only because others work hard for little thanks?' Say: 'Dignity of labour means every kind of honest work deserves respect.'

steps.title: Choose one real change
steps.do: From the audit, your child chooses one problem to really fix this week (for example: separate the bins, fix a drip, plant three saplings, switch off unused fans, thank and learn the name of the person who cleans). Write a simple plan: what, who, how we'll measure it, and a date to check. This is the heart of the project.

days.title: The warm jar
days.goal: Trap heat in a jar, meet Eunice Foote, and see why white ice melts slower.

steps.title: Greenhouse in a jar
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Put a thermometer inside each of two identical clear jars. In one jar, a grown-up mixes a spoon of baking soda with a little vinegar at the bottom. It fizzes and fills the jar with carbon dioxide gas. Wait until the fizzing stops and both thermometers show the same temperature. Close both jars and put them side by side in the same strong sunlight. Ask: 'Will one jar get warmer than the other? Why?' Read both thermometers every 5 minutes for 15 minutes. Often the carbon dioxide jar warms a little more. Say honestly: 'In a small jar the difference is small, and sometimes there is none. But the Earth has kilometres of air above it. There, carbon dioxide keeps our planet warm, and the extra carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and wood makes it warmer.'

steps.title: The woman who got there first
steps.do: Talk about voice v3, Eunice Foote. Ask: 'Why do you think her paper was read by a man? Why might a later scientist get the credit?' Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: A prediction made with pencil and paper
steps.do: Tell your child: 'In 1896 a Swedish scientist, Svante Arrhenius, spent many months doing sums by hand and predicted that burning coal would slowly warm the whole Earth. He got the direction right. But he thought it would take thousands of years, and might even be pleasant for cold Sweden. It has happened much faster, because we burn far more than he imagined.' Ask: 'Can a scientist be right and wrong at the same time?'

steps.title: Ice on black and white
steps.do: Put an ice cube on a black cloth and one on a white cloth in the sun. Ask: 'Which will melt first?' Check after 5 minutes. Then ask: 'What happens to the Earth when white ice and snow melt and leave dark sea and rock?' (The dark surfaces absorb more sunlight, so the Earth warms more, so more ice melts. Scientists call this kind of loop a feedback loop.)

need: two thermometers (room thermometers are cheap at a medical or hardware shop)
two ice cubes, a black cloth and a white cloth

days.title: Nature has no borders
days.goal: Follow the falcons, the seeds and the food that cross the world.

steps.title: Back to Doyang
steps.do: Go back to the story. Ask: 'Which countries does an Amur falcon depend on in one year?' (Mongolia, China or Russia, where they nest. India, where they rest and feed. Countries in southern Africa, where they spend the winter. And the sea in between.) Ask: 'If one country protects the falcons and another doesn't, what happens?'

steps.title: The falcon's map
steps.do: On a world map (an atlas page, or one you draw), your child draws the Amur falcons' journey: from north-east Asia south to Nagaland, then across the Arabian Sea to Africa, and back in spring. Add other travellers. Rosy starlings fly from Central Asia and eat locusts in Indian fields. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas. Winds carry dust from the Thar desert across north India. Ask: 'Which of these travellers needs a passport?'

steps.title: Foods and ideas that travelled
steps.do: Ask: 'Which of these foods are Indian: chilli, potato, tomato, tea, sugar, rice?' Then tell them. Chilli, potato and tomato came from the Americas only about 500 years ago. The British started tea gardens in India in the 1800s, with plants from China and a wild tea that the Singpho people of Assam already drank. Sugar crystals were first made from sugarcane in India, and then travelled the world. Rice was first grown in Asia. Ideas travel too: yoga and the way of writing numbers with a zero spread from India, and paper came from China. Ask: 'Does anything belong to only one country?'

steps.title: Planet Keepers
steps.do: Play the cooperative board game g1. Everyone wins or loses together.

need: the printed game board, a die, counters

days.title: One family
days.goal: Meet the old idea that the whole Earth is one family, and a modern scientific idea that Earth behaves like one living system.

steps.title: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam
steps.do: Tell your child the meaning of an old Sanskrit verse from the Maha Upanishad: 'This is mine, that is a stranger's: so think the small-minded. For the large-hearted, the whole Earth is one family.' Explain that 'vasudha' means the Earth and 'kutumbakam' means family. Ask: 'Does the family include only people? Who else would you put in it?' (Falcons, rivers, soil creatures, trees.) Ask: 'What does a family do when one member is in trouble?'

steps.title: Is the Earth alive?
steps.do: Talk about voice v4, Lovelock and Margulis and the Gaia idea. Ask: 'Is the Earth alive? What would it need to do to count as alive?' (Use the signs of life from earlier classes: does it grow, take in energy, keep itself steady, reproduce?) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Drama: the Earth council
steps.do: Hold a council. Each person plays a part of the Earth system: the Sun, the sea, the forests, the soil, the ice, the air, the falcons, and the people. The question: 'The people want to burn more coal to make more things. What does each of you say?' Each speaker says what they give, what they need, and what happens to them if the people burn more coal. Then the people must reply. Ask afterwards: 'Did anyone change their mind?'

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2: forests, heat and the shared Earth in new places.

days.title: Pledge, check and teach it back
days.goal: Report on the real change, try the challenge worksheet, and write a letter to the future.

steps.title: What did we change?
steps.do: Your child reports on the one real change from Day 5: what we did, what we measured, whether it worked, and what we'd do next. Ask: 'What was harder than you expected? Who helped?'

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last questions have no single right answer: ask for evidence and reasons.

steps.title: Check questions
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Let your child use the hill model, the soil drawings and the falcon map to explain.

steps.title: Teach it back, and a letter to 2075
steps.do: Your child teaches the family in five minutes: how soil is lost and saved, why forests matter, and what the greenhouse jar showed. Then they write a short letter to a child living in 2075, saying what the Earth is like now, one thing their family did, and one question they would like to ask that child.

experiments.title: Wind on dry, damp and covered soil
experiments.question: Which soil does the wind carry away most easily?
steps: Make three equal heaps: dry soil, damp soil, and dry soil covered with dry leaves.
Spread newspaper around each plate.
Blow through the straw at each heap for 10 seconds, from the same distance.
Look at how far the soil has spread on the paper.
Compare and write down what you saw.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which heap will lose the most soil?'
experiments.observe: The dry, bare heap spreads widely. The damp heap and the covered heap lose little.
experiments.why: Dry, loose soil grains have nothing holding them, so wind lifts them. Water sticks grains together, and leaves shield the surface. That is why bare, ploughed fields lose so much topsoil in dry, windy seasons, and why rows of trees and cover crops protect farms.
experiments.safety: Blow away from faces. Wash hands after.

experiments.title: How much life is in a handful of soil?
experiments.question: Is soil where dead leaves lie more alive than bare, dry soil?
need: two handfuls of soil: one from a plant pot or from under a tree where dead leaves lie, one from a bare, swept corner or roadside
a magnifying glass, or the zoom on a phone camera
steps: Spread each handful on its own white paper.
Look for 5 minutes at each, gently moving the soil with a stick.
Count and draw every living thing.
Put the soil and creatures back where they came from.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which handful will have more living things?'
experiments.observe: The soil with dead leaves usually has ants, springtails, mites, small worms or white fungus threads. The bare, dry soil has few or none. If you find few creatures in both, look for white threads and bits of rotting leaf: these are signs of life too.
experiments.why: Soil creatures eat dead leaves and each other. Where leaves are left to rot, there is food. The creatures mix the soil, make tunnels for air and water, and release nutrients for plants. Bare, swept or poisoned soil has little food and few creatures, so it gets hard and poor.
experiments.safety: Use a stick, not bare hands, and wash hands after. Don't touch centipedes, because they can bite.

experiments.title: Black paper, white paper, shade
experiments.question: How do colour and shade change how hot a surface gets?
need: a second sheet of black paper
a sunny balcony or windowsill in the late morning
steps: Put the black and white sheets side by side in full sun.
Put the second black sheet in the shade nearby.
Wait 15 minutes.
Feel each with the back of your hand.
If you go out, also feel a tarred road in the sun and the ground under a tree.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will be hottest? Will the black paper in the shade get hot?'
experiments.observe: The black sheet in the sun is hottest. The white sheet in the sun is cooler. The black sheet in the shade is coolest. A road in the sun is much hotter than the ground under a tree.
experiments.why: Dark surfaces absorb most of the sunlight that falls on them and turn it into heat. White surfaces reflect most of it. Trees block sunlight, and they also cool the air, because water evaporates from their leaves, and evaporation takes heat away. Cities full of dark roads and roofs and few trees become heat islands.
experiments.safety: Don't touch very hot surfaces with your palm; test with the back of your hand quickly.

experiments.title: Greenhouse in a jar
experiments.question: Does air with more carbon dioxide warm up faster in sunlight?
need: two identical clear jars or bottles
two thermometers (room thermometers are cheap at a medical or hardware shop)
steps: Put a thermometer in each jar, facing out so you can read it.
In one jar, a grown-up adds a spoon of baking soda and a little vinegar.
Wait until the fizzing stops and both thermometers show the same temperature.
Close both jars, and put them side by side in the same strong sunlight.
Read both every 5 minutes for 15 minutes, and write the numbers down.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will one jar get warmer than the other?'
experiments.observe: Both jars warm up. The carbon dioxide jar often warms a little more, by about 1 or 2 degrees. The difference is small, and shade, wind or a loose lid can hide it. If you see no difference, that is a real result: write it down.
experiments.why: Sunlight passes through air and warms the ground. The warm ground gives off invisible heat, called infrared. Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb some of that heat and keep it in. This is the greenhouse effect. Without it, the Earth would be frozen. Burning coal, oil and wood adds more carbon dioxide, so more heat is kept in. Eunice Foote showed the first hint of this in 1856, with glass cylinders much like these jars.
experiments.safety: Vinegar and baking soda only; no flames. Don't drink from the jars.

activities.title: A hill farm that holds its soil
need: a plastic bottle with holes in the cap
steps: Build two hills the same size, one on each tray.
Tilt each tray on a book, with a cup at the low end.
Leave one hill smooth and bare.
On the other, press in terraces with the ruler.
Add rows of pebbles across the slope, and a small stone wall across a channel.
Stick in twigs and grass as trees and cover.
Pour the same amount of 'rain' on both, and compare the mud in the cups.
activities.outcome: Two models that show how terraces, bunds, check dams and plants hold soil.

activities.title: The green audit
need: an audit sheet with five sections
steps: Waste: count bins, check if wet and dry are separate.
Water: look for drips and see if rain is caught.
Energy: count lights and fans on in empty rooms; check bulb types.
Greenery: count trees and plants; note bare soil.
People: find out who cleans and repairs, and whether everyone has a safe, shady place.
Score each section 1–5 and write one problem for each.
activities.outcome: A scored audit of your place and a list of problems to fix.

voices.who: Hugh Hammond Bennett (1881–1960), soil scientist, USA
voices.idea: Bennett studied farms all over the USA and saw that ploughed, bare fields were losing their topsoil to rain and wind. In 1928 he wrote a report called 'Soil Erosion: A National Menace'. In the 1930s, after the grasslands of the Great Plains had been ploughed up for wheat, a long drought came, and the bare soil blew away in enormous dust storms: the Dust Bowl. Bennett argued that farmers must keep soil covered, plough across slopes instead of up and down them, and plant windbreaks of trees.
voices.then: Many people believed soil was endless and that erosion didn't matter much. It is told that in 1935, while Bennett was speaking to the US Congress, a dust storm from the Great Plains, more than 2,000 km away, darkened the sky over Washington. Soon after, the government set up a Soil Conservation Service with Bennett as its head.
voices.now: Accepted. Soil erosion is now known as one of the biggest threats to farming worldwide, and the methods Bennett pushed for are used everywhere.
voices.ask: Before the dust storm, many people didn't believe Bennett. Why is it hard to believe a warning about something that happens slowly? What would convince you?

voices.who: The organic versus chemical farming debate: the Green Revolution, Sikkim (2016) and Sri Lanka (2021)
voices.idea: From the 1960s, India's Green Revolution, led by scientists such as M.S. Swaminathan, used new seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation, and India went from food shortages to growing enough grain to feed itself. But in places like Punjab, years of heavy chemical use and pumping have harmed soil, polluted water and lowered groundwater. Organic farming uses compost, manure and natural pest control instead. In 2016 Sikkim became India's first fully organic state, changing slowly over more than ten years. In 2021 Sri Lanka banned chemical fertilisers suddenly, almost overnight.
voices.then: Supporters of chemicals say the world can't be fed without them. Supporters of organic farming say chemicals are killing the soil we depend on.
voices.now: Debated. In Sri Lanka, harvests of rice and tea fell sharply and the ban was reversed within months. Sikkim's slower change has kept going, but its yields and farmers' incomes are still being studied. Many scientists now argue for a mix: using much less chemical, carefully, with more compost and soil life.
voices.ask: Sikkim changed slowly and Sri Lanka changed suddenly. Why might the speed of a change matter as much as the change itself?

voices.who: Eunice Newton Foote (1819–1888), scientist and women's rights campaigner, USA
voices.idea: In 1856 Foote put thermometers in glass cylinders filled with different gases (ordinary air, damp air, dry air, carbon dioxide) and set them in sunlight. The cylinder with carbon dioxide got the hottest and stayed hot longest. She wrote that an atmosphere with more of that gas would give the Earth a higher temperature. This was the first written hint of the greenhouse effect and of climate change.
voices.then: Her paper was read aloud at a big science meeting by a man, Joseph Henry, and was soon forgotten. Three years later, in 1859, the Irish scientist John Tyndall did more detailed experiments on how gases absorb heat and was credited for over a century. There is no evidence he knew of her work.
voices.now: Accepted, and her credit is being restored. Her paper was rediscovered around 2010, and she is now often called the first person to show that carbon dioxide traps heat. Tyndall's careful work was also important: it showed it was invisible heat from the ground, not sunlight itself, that the gases trap.
voices.ask: Foote's paper was read by a man and then forgotten. How many other discoveries might be lost like that? How could we find them?

voices.who: James Lovelock (1919–2022) and Lynn Margulis (1938–2011): the Gaia idea
voices.idea: In the 1970s the British scientist James Lovelock, working with the American biologist Lynn Margulis, proposed that living things and the rocks, air and oceans together act like one huge self-regulating system that keeps the Earth suitable for life, for example by keeping the oxygen in the air and the saltiness of the sea fairly steady. Lovelock named it Gaia, after the Greek Earth goddess. Margulis brought the knowledge of microbes and how they change the air and soil.
voices.then: Many biologists attacked it, saying that evolution could not make the whole planet work 'on purpose', and that it sounded more like a religion than science.
voices.now: Debated. The strong version (the Earth is a living thing that keeps itself in balance on purpose) is not accepted by most scientists. But the weaker version, that life and the planet shape each other in loops (microbes made the oxygen in our air; forests make rain), is now the basis of a whole field called Earth system science.
voices.ask: What would the Earth need to do for you to call it alive? Is it enough that it keeps itself steady?

project.title: Green explorers: one real change
steps: Audit your home, building or school for waste, water, energy, greenery and people (Day 5).
Score each section and write one problem for each.
Choose one problem to fix this week and write a plan: what, who, how we'll measure it, a date to check.
Do it every day for at least four days, and measure (litres saved, bags separated, saplings watered, units on the meter).
Talk to the people affected, including the person who cleans.
Report: what you did, what you measured, what worked, what you'd do next (Day 9).
project.outcome: A real, measured change to your own place, and a report on it.

game.title: Planet Keepers
rules: This is a cooperative game: everyone plays as one team and wins or loses together.
Start with 10 soil tokens in the 'healthy Earth' pile.
Take turns to roll the die and move the team counter.
Read the square aloud. A harm square takes away tokens; a care square gives them back. Before acting, the player must say why the square helps or harms.
On a harm square, the team may spend one turn to 'fix it' instead of moving, if someone can explain a real way to prevent it: then no tokens are lost.
The team wins by reaching ONE FAMILY with at least 5 tokens. If the tokens run out, everyone loses and starts again.
squares: START: the blue planet
A forest is cut on a steep hill: lose 2
Farmers build terraces: gain 1
Plastic dumped in a field: lose 1
A village builds a check dam: gain 1
Bare fields in a dust storm: lose 2
Compost instead of too much fertiliser: gain 1
Falcons netted on their journey: lose 1
A village protects the falcons: gain 2
A city paints roofs white: gain 1
Coal smoke fills the air: lose 2
Forest people keep their sacred grove: gain 1
Pesticide kills the soil creatures: lose 1
Leaves left to rot under trees: gain 1
A heat wave in a treeless city: lose 1
Neighbours plant shade trees: gain 1
Someone thanks the person who cleans: gain 1
Ice melts and the sea warms: lose 1
Two countries agree to share a river: gain 2
ONE FAMILY: the whole Earth

story.title: The Sky Over Doyang
text: Every October, the sky over Achumi's village filled with falcons.

They came from nowhere, it seemed. One evening the sky above the Doyang reservoir was empty and blue, and the next it was full of small grey birds, more than anyone could count, swirling over the water and the forest like smoke, settling on the trees until the branches bent. They were Amur falcons, though nobody in Pangti called them that. They called them the October birds. Their wings made a sound like rain.

Achumi was ten, and she lived in Pangti, a village of the Lotha Naga people on the hills of Wokha in Nagaland. Her uncle Yanbemo set nets for the falcons. Most families did. The nets were long and fine, strung between bamboo poles near the roosting trees, and in the morning they were heavy with birds. The birds went to the market in sacks. For a few weeks every year, the falcons brought more money into the village than anything else. Achumi's school fees came from the falcons. So did her new red sweater.
She had never thought much about it. The falcons came, the nets went up, the money came. It was like the rain.

But that year, early one morning, she went with her uncle to the nets. In a corner where the net had sagged into a bush, she found one bird still alive, caught by one wing, struggling. He was smaller than she expected, smaller than a pigeon, with a grey back, orange legs and an orange ring around each eye. He stopped struggling when she touched him. He looked at her, very still.
Without quite knowing why, she slipped him inside her red sweater and carried him home.

She kept him for three days in an old basket in the cowshed. She gave him rice, which he ignored, and water, which he drank. On the second day, after a rain shower, a swarm of winged termites rose from the ground. She held the basket open, and the falcon caught them one after another out of the air, faster than she could see, and ate them. So that was what he lived on. Not rice. Insects, caught in the air.

On the third day a visitor came to the village school: a young woman from a wildlife group, with a laptop and a map. She talked to the children about the October birds. Some of the children giggled, and some of the older ones looked angry, because they knew what she was going to say. But Achumi listened.

She showed them a map of the world. She put her finger on Mongolia, and China, and the far east of Russia. 'This is where your October birds are born,' she said. 'In summer, up here, they nest and raise their chicks.' Then she drew a line, down across China, across Myanmar, to a tiny dot that was Nagaland. 'In autumn they come here. They rest in your forests for a few weeks and eat the insects, and get fat and strong.' Then she drew the line on, out over India, and out over the sea, the whole wide blue of the Arabian Sea, all the way to Africa. 'They cross that sea without stopping,' she said. 'Day and night, for days. No land. Nowhere to rest. Then they spend the winter in southern Africa, and in spring they fly all the way back.'
'Why do they come to us?' a boy asked.
'Because you have what they need,' the young woman said. 'Forests to sleep in, water, and insects to eat, at just the right time, just before the hardest part of the journey.'

Achumi went home and sat beside the basket and looked at the falcon for a long time. She thought about the line on the map. She thought about the nest in Mongolia, which she would never see, and the chicks in it. She thought about a boy in Africa who would look up in December and see these same birds, and maybe call them the December birds. She thought about the sea, so big that the falcon must fly for days over it without a single branch to sit on. This little grey bird, who fitted inside her sweater, belonged to Mongolia, and to Nagaland, and to Africa, and to the sea. He belonged to everyone along the line. He did not belong to her uncle's net.

She took the basket to the edge of the forest above the reservoir that evening, when the sky was full of swirling falcons. She opened it. The falcon did not move for a moment. Then he was gone, so fast she didn't see him go, and she couldn't tell which one he was among the thousands.
She told her uncle what she had done. She thought he would be angry. He was quiet for a long time.

That winter there were meetings in the village, long ones, with arguments and shouting. Some people said the falcons were a gift and the money was needed. Some said the whole country was ashamed of Pangti. Some said the falcons were guests, and that in Naga tradition you do not kill a guest. In the end the village councils of Pangti and the villages around it made a rule: no more nets. Some of the men who had been the best trappers became the falcon guards.

The next October, the sky over Doyang filled with falcons again, and the nets did not go up. People came from all over India, and from other countries, to see them. The village earned money from the visitors instead.

And that year, the scientists fitted a few of the falcons with tiny satellite tags, as light as a coin, and named them after the places that had protected them. On the school laptop, Achumi watched a little dot leave Nagaland, cross India, and set out over the blue of the Arabian Sea, and she watched it all day, and all the next day, until it touched the coast of Africa, and she let out her breath.
story.epiphany: Achumi sees the falcon as a village resource, something that comes like the rain and brings money. The turn comes with the map: the bird is born in Mongolia, rests in Nagaland, crosses the sea to Africa. She understands that it belongs to everyone along its route, and to no one's net. The hidden idea is that nature has no borders: one bird joins many countries and depends on habitats in all of them (forests, insects, water), so the Earth is one shared home. The quiet lenses: the falcons are 'guests'; the trappers become guards; the village finds another way to earn; nobody is turned into a villain.
ask: Why did the falcons stop in Achumi's village?
Whose bird was the falcon? Why did Achumi decide it didn't belong to the net?
Why might the village have needed the falcon money? Was it fair to ask them to stop?
What changed the uncle's mind, do you think?
Why did Achumi hold her breath while she watched the dot cross the sea?

ideas.idea: Soil is a thin, living layer that took a very long time to make.
ideas.more: A few centimetres of topsoil can take hundreds of years to form, and can wash or blow away in one season. The hill models and the soil count show how plants and soil creatures keep soil in place and alive.

ideas.idea: Birds, winds and seeds cross every border.
ideas.more: Falcons, starlings, winds, dust, rain and seeds cross borders all the time. One bird can depend on forests in three continents. What one country does to its air or its forests reaches everyone.

ideas.idea: Air we can't see keeps the Earth warm.
ideas.more: Carbon dioxide and water vapour trap heat, as Eunice Foote's jars showed. Without them Earth would freeze; with too much added, it warms.

ideas.idea: A place is only green if it is good for everyone in it.
ideas.more: The green audit includes the people who clean and repair, the trees and the creatures. Kindness, respect and dignity of labour are part of caring for a place, not separate from it.

unknowns: How much topsoil is the world really losing each year, and how fast is new soil forming? Estimates vary widely, because soil is hard to measure over large areas and long times.

How does an Amur falcon find their way across the open sea, thousands of kilometres with no land in sight? Scientists think birds may use the Sun, the stars and the Earth's magnetism, but nobody fully understands how.
Is the Earth in some sense a living system that keeps itself in balance? Scientists still argue about how far the Gaia idea is true.
big: If the whole Earth is one family, who is in the family?
Who should decide what happens to a forest: the people who live in it, the government, a company, or the animals?
Is a place green if it is clean for some people because others work hard for little thanks?
Should a country be allowed to do whatever it wants with its own air, if the air flows to everyone?
Can a scientist be right and wrong at the same time?

challenge.q: 'The Amazon rainforest is the lungs of the Earth and makes 20% of our oxygen.'
challenge.hint: The Amazon's plants do make huge amounts of oxygen, but the forest's animals, fungi and microbes use up almost all of it again, so its overall gift of oxygen is close to zero. Most of the oxygen built up in our air over millions of years came from tiny plants in the ocean. The Amazon matters enormously for other reasons: it stores vast carbon, makes much of South America's rain and is home to millions of kinds of life. Ask: why do people like simple slogans? Does the real reason matter?

challenge.q: 'Planting a trillion trees will solve climate change.'
challenge.hint: A famous 2019 study suggested the world had room for about a trillion more trees, which could store a large amount of carbon. Other scientists replied that it had overestimated the space and the carbon, that trees in the wrong places (grasslands, snowy lands) can harm wildlife or even warm the Earth, and that trees take decades to grow. Protecting the forests we already have, and burning less coal and oil, matter most. Ask: why might a big, simple solution be attractive?

challenge.q: 'Chillies, potatoes and tomatoes are traditional Indian foods.'
challenge.hint: They are deeply Indian now, but they all came from the Americas, carried by Portuguese and other traders only about 500 years ago. Before that, Indian food got its heat from black pepper and long pepper. Ask: how long does something have to be here to belong here?

perspectives.view: For over 500 years the Bishnois have followed rules that forbid cutting green trees and harming animals, and the blackbuck and chinkara still roam near their villages. Ask: what makes a rule last 500 years?

perspectives.who: A tea or cardamom farmer in the Western Ghats
perspectives.view: On steep hills, the forest above the farm holds the soil and keeps the springs flowing. When the forest is cleared, landslides come in heavy monsoons. Ask: is the forest above the farm part of the farm?

Earthworms swallow soil and dead leaves, and leave behind rich droppings called casts. Their tunnels let air and rain into the soil. A field with many earthworms needs less ploughing. Ask: if earthworms could audit our garden, what score would they give it?
From space, he saw no borders, only one blue planet. Ask: why might seeing the whole Earth at once change how a person feels about it?

books.title: Seeds of Change: Wangari's Gift to the World
books.author: Jen Cullerton Johnson
books.why: Wangari Maathai's life, from a girl in Kenya to the woman whose tree-planters fought soil erosion and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

books.title: The Great Kapok Tree
books.author: Lynne Cherry
books.why: The animals of the rainforest each explain to a sleeping woodcutter why their tree matters: a gentle way into 'why forests matter'.

books.title: Dirt: The Scoop on Soil
books.author: Natalie Myra Rosinsky
books.why: How soil is made, its layers, and the creatures in it. Good before the handful-of-soil count.

books.title: Silent Spring
books.author: Rachel Carson
books.age: adult book; read short parts aloud
books.why: The book that showed how poisons spread through soil, water and living things.

check.q: What is topsoil and why is it precious?
check.a: The dark top layer of soil full of humus and life where plants grow; it takes hundreds of years to form and can be lost quickly.

check.q: How do water and wind cause soil erosion?
check.a: Rain and running water wash loose soil down slopes and into rivers; wind blows dry, bare soil away.

check.q: Name four ways to prevent soil erosion.
check.a: Terraces, bunds, check dams, keeping soil covered with plants or mulch, planting trees and windbreaks.

check.q: What pollutes soil, and what keeps it healthy?
check.a: Plastic, pesticides, too much chemical fertiliser, factory waste; compost, manure, leaf litter and soil creatures keep it healthy.

check.q: Give three reasons forests must be protected.
check.a: For example: they hold soil, feed springs and rivers, cool the air, store carbon, and are home to animals and forest people.

check.q: What did Eunice Foote's experiment show?
check.a: That air with carbon dioxide heats up more in sunlight: the greenhouse effect.

check.q: Why does the Amur falcon show that nature has no borders?
check.a: It nests in north-east Asia, rests in Nagaland and winters in Africa, depending on habitats in many countries.
The whole Earth is one family.
